Either option is acceptable: remove the 44Ω resistors if they complicate the layout, or leave them in place if they are already fitted and not obstructing anything.

Those resistors on SDA/SCL are only there for signal quality. Because I2C lines are open-drain, releasing them requires the pull-up resistor to recharge the cable capacitance to 3.3V. That can produce slight overshoot or ringing at the transition edge, which the series resistance damps.

With our 20–40cm cables and 4.4kΩ pull-ups, rise time will remain well within specification, so this should not be a meaningful problem.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
With the main board in the middle, the three boards are chained in this order: power board → main board → sensor board. Power reaches the main board from the power board through J\_PWR\_PWR, is consumed locally, and is also forwarded through J\_SENSOR\_PWR to the sensor board. It works like a power strip: power arrives through one cable, supplies the main board's own components, and continues to the sensor board via a second cable.
Immediately after the Schottky diodes, the INA219 sits in series on the 3.3V rail. It therefore measures the total 3.3V current for everything downstream—the ESP32 itself plus whatever the sensor board draws—in one reading.

Here is the power mapping by operating mode:

With the power board connected, the primary source is the 3.3V rail (AXP2101 DCDC1, 3.5A). It powers:
- ESP32-S3 module
- INA219
- all I2C sensors on the sensor board: SCD41, BME280, and ENS160
- I2C display
- TTP223 and AM312 PIR

Controlled by ESP32 GPIO3, the 5V rail (MT3608 boost, 1200mA) powers:
- SPS30 particulate sensor
- ZE08-CH2O formaldehyde sensor
- SK6812 LEDs, but only if they are wired to 5V; that depends on the version

When USB-C is connected to the main board while the power board is absent, the 3.3V rail (ME6211A LDO, 2A) becomes active for standalone programming. It supplies the same 3.3V rail listed above; Schottky diode OR-ing allows whichever source is present to take precedence.

The 2.8–4.6V battery feeds AXP2101, which then supplies everything downstream.

In short, AXP2101 powers everything during normal operation; the LDO activates only for programming without the power board connected.

After reviewing the schematic and PCB files closely, I think the board looks solid overall and the work is good. Could you examine these observations and share your thoughts?

1\. For the USB-C connector (USB1), DRC reports hole-clearance violations and negative annular width on the 2 mounting pin holes. The drills appear larger than their copper pads. Will JLCPCB accept the footprint as it is, or must it be fixed?

3. Although D1 is marked DNP, its current-limiting resistor R6 (4.7k) remains in the BOM and would be assembled. With D1 unplaced, one R6 pin would float. Is there a reason to retain R6, or should R6 also be DNP?
4. To avoid confusion, the VSIS net name is worth correcting because it appears to be a typo for VSYS.
5\. For L1, DRC says the Inductor_SMD:L_Changjiang_FTC404020S footprint is absent from the standard KiCad library and uses a local override. Please confirm that its physical dimensions match the intended 4.7uH inductor.

value_updates.vmid_vsys_reference_conformance: The VMID and VSYS topology must be verified against the AXP2101 datasheet or an applicable reference design.

requirements.title: Integrated-Board DCDC1 Regulation and Load Stability

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hi Luka,

After the rework—removing U3 and bridging the data lines—USB is now fully operational; the boards enumerate correctly and can be flashed. Testing the power system and AXP2101 on both boards produced identical results:

1\. DCDC1 idles at 3.16V. The register is confirmed at 3.3V (0x82 reads 0x12), so the converter regulates 4 percent low.
2\. Every load transient collapses the rail. A SPI flash erase with an approximately 150mA step or a WiFi TX burst of 300-400mA pulls the 3.3V rail below 2.5V and hard-resets the ESP32. Disabling the brown-out detector changes nothing because the rail itself is genuinely collapsing, and adding 330uF of external capacitance does not help. The board therefore cannot operate standalone from USB.
3\. Battery-only operation succeeds with VSYS around 3.8V, whereas a 5V USB input causes failure. In other words, the problem appears exactly when the buck must regulate, while operation near dropout survives.
4\. Programming DCDC1 to 3.4V through I2C improves matters substantially: booting, WiFi service, and a complete 1.9MB OTA write all succeed. The calibration surge from WiFi during reboot still collapses the rail, however. Another oddity is that the 0x82 write was ignored on several boots, with readback remaining 0x12, before it latched during a later boot. Other register writes verify correctly. Because the default VBUS input-current limit is 1.5A, input limiting is not the cause.
5\. I substituted L3 with a physically larger 2.2uH inductor rated for much higher saturation current, but the behavior did not change at all. The inductor is not responsible, and the original DFE252010F specification was adequate.
6\. Further testing caused DCDC1 on board 2 to deteriorate progressively before failing completely. With everything else disconnected, its output now measures about 265 ohm to GND, indicating leakage in the output stage.
7\. Supplying the board externally at 3.3V keeps the entire system working perfectly for hours. Boot, PSRAM, e-paper, WiFi, the web UI, and the sensors all operate correctly, so the downstream circuitry is healthy.

My current conclusion is that the AXP2101 devices themselves may be suspect because of a bad batch, counterfeit components, moisture damage during reflow, or non-standard factory programming. I have asked the factory for sourcing details and lot codes. On your side, one useful check would be the local input decoupling at the DCDC1 VIN pins: is a capacitor placed close to those pins, or is there only the more distant bulk group?

Can you think of another explanation consistent with all these findings?

execution.observed_behavior: DCDC1 regulated low at 3.16V and collapsed below 2.5V during flash and WiFi load transients, hard-resetting the ESP32; a 3.4V setting improved operation but did not prevent the WiFi reboot surge from collapsing the rail, and one converter eventually failed completely.

source_message.speaker: client
source_message.text:
Hi Luka,

After the rework—removing U3 and bridging the data lines—USB is now fully operational; the boards enumerate correctly and can be flashed. Testing the power system and AXP2101 on both boards produced identical results:

1\. DCDC1 idles at 3.16V. The register is confirmed at 3.3V (0x82 reads 0x12), so the converter regulates 4 percent low.
2\. Every load transient collapses the rail. A SPI flash erase with an approximately 150mA step or a WiFi TX burst of 300-400mA pulls the 3.3V rail below 2.5V and hard-resets the ESP32. Disabling the brown-out detector changes nothing because the rail itself is genuinely collapsing, and adding 330uF of external capacitance does not help. The board therefore cannot operate standalone from USB.
3\. Battery-only operation succeeds with VSYS around 3.8V, whereas a 5V USB input causes failure. In other words, the problem appears exactly when the buck must regulate, while operation near dropout survives.
4\. Programming DCDC1 to 3.4V through I2C improves matters substantially: booting, WiFi service, and a complete 1.9MB OTA write all succeed. The calibration surge from WiFi during reboot still collapses the rail, however. Another oddity is that the 0x82 write was ignored on several boots, with readback remaining 0x12, before it latched during a later boot. Other register writes verify correctly. Because the default VBUS input-current limit is 1.5A, input limiting is not the cause.
5\. I substituted L3 with a physically larger 2.2uH inductor rated for much higher saturation current, but the behavior did not change at all. The inductor is not responsible, and the original DFE252010F specification was adequate.
6\. Further testing caused DCDC1 on board 2 to deteriorate progressively before failing completely. With everything else disconnected, its output now measures about 265 ohm to GND, indicating leakage in the output stage.
7\. Supplying the board externally at 3.3V keeps the entire system working perfectly for hours. Boot, PSRAM, e-paper, WiFi, the web UI, and the sensors all operate correctly, so the downstream circuitry is healthy.

My current conclusion is that the AXP2101 devices themselves may be suspect because of a bad batch, counterfeit components, moisture damage during reflow, or non-standard factory programming. I have asked the factory for sourcing details and lot codes. On your side, one useful check would be the local input decoupling at the DCDC1 VIN pins: is a capacitor placed close to those pins, or is there only the more distant bulk group?

Can you think of another explanation consistent with all these findings?

execution.observed_behavior: With 5V USB input, load transients collapse the 3.3V rail below 2.5V and reset the ESP32, preventing standalone USB operation without a battery; battery-only operation succeeds.

source_message.text:
Thanks, Luka. Everything is clear:
1. For v4, leave VRTC NC because this board has no external RTC chip. On the RTC topic, I realized that I previously mixed up VRTC with VBACKUP. VBACKUP (pin 27) supplies backup power to keep the AXP2101's internal RTC running after the main battery is removed. Could you expose VBACKUP on a small test pad or via beside PWROK from item #10? This would let us later install a 200 µF capacitor for \~8-10 min of hot-swap tolerance, a supercap for several weeks, or a CR1220 coin cell for \~9 years of real time-keeping. Nothing needs to be populated now; only expose the pad.
2. For the buttons (R16/R17/R18), agreed: convert all three to pull-ups at 3V3. They remain active LOW, with connector pin 1 tied to GND and a press shorting the GPIO input to GND. I updated <http://board-package.example|pcb-integrated.md> to reflect this.
3. The PIR (R19) and Touch (R20/R25) circuits are already correct as pull-downs and need no changes. Both the AM312 (PIR) and TTP223 (touch) provide push-pull active-HIGH outputs, so their internal drivers override the 20 k pull-down while active. The pull-down to GND simply ensures a defined LOW state whenever a sensor is unplugged.
